a: Such stones! Such buildings!
p: The disciple was right to be amazed: some of Herod's Temple stones were the largest building blocks in the Roman world.
b: Herod the Great rebuilt the Temple and its platform from about 20 BC, and work went on until the 60s AD. Josephus describes stones of enormous size and a sanctuary faced with gold that shone in the sun. Blocks still visible in the Western Wall run to about 40 feet (12 meters) long. A village disciple from Galilee had never seen anything like it. Matthew 24:1 has the disciples as a group; Mark gives one voice and the word "Teacher." On Herod's Temple and the history of the building, see the notes at Matthew 24:1.

a: not one stone will be left on a stone
p: Roman soldiers burned the Temple in August AD 70 and later tore down its buildings.
b: Titus's army took Jerusalem in AD 70. Josephus, who watched, says the sanctuary burned and the city was later leveled except for a few towers and part of a wall. Huge stones thrown down from the Temple platform still lie on the Herodian street at the southwest corner. Whether Jesus foresaw this, or whether Mark wrote after it happened, is one of the main questions for dating the Gospel (see the deep dive on this chapter page). Matthew 24:2 has the same saying; its notes cover Jewish memory of the fall.

a: across from the temple
p: Jesus sits facing the Temple, like a judge, on the hill where Zechariah saw the LORD standing on the last day.
b: From the Mount of Olives a person looks straight across the Kidron Valley at the Temple. Mark alone says Jesus sat "across from" it (κατέναντι). He has just left the building for the last time (13:1) after condemning its leaders (11:15–17; 12:38–40). Sitting was the posture of a teacher and of a judge. Many readers also hear Zechariah 14:4, where the LORD's feet stand on the Mount of Olives on the day of the LORD, and Ezekiel 11:23, where God's glory leaves the Temple and stops on the mountain east of the city.

a: Peter, James, John and Andrew
p: Only Mark names who heard the speech: the first four disciples Jesus called.
b: Matthew says "the disciples" and Luke has a public crowd. Mark names the two pairs of brothers whose call opened Jesus' ministry (1:16–20). Three of them also saw Jairus's daughter raised (5:37) and the transfiguration (9:2), and three will be taken into Gethsemane (14:33). The private setting fits a pattern in Mark, where hard teaching is explained "by themselves" (4:10, 34; 9:28). The speech ends with "what I tell you, I tell everyone" (13:37), so Mark shows a private warning that is meant for every reader.

a: all these things are about to be completed
p: In Mark the disciples ask only about the Temple. Matthew adds a question about Jesus' coming and the end of the age.
b: Mark's two questions both look back to Jesus' word about the stones: when, and what sign? The verb (συντελεῖσθαι, "be brought to completion") echoes Daniel 12:7 in the Greek, where "all these things" are completed. Matthew 24:3 widens the question to "your coming and the completion of the age," which is one reason readers of Matthew often split the speech into two subjects. In Mark the answer moves from the Temple (13:5–23) to the coming of the Son of Man (13:24–27), and readers still disagree on whether Mark joins them or keeps them apart. See the four ways of reading the speech at Matthew 24.

a: Be on your guard
p: The Greek verb blepete, "watch, look out," comes four times. The speech is a call to watchfulness, not a timetable.
b: "Be on your guard" here and in 13:9, 23 and 33 renders the same Greek command, βλέπετε, "look, watch out." It is joined at the end by "stay alert" and three times "stay awake" (13:33–37). The pattern shows what the speech is for. The disciples asked when; Jesus answers mostly with how to live: do not be fooled, do not panic, hold out, run when it is time, keep awake. Many interpreters, whatever they think the prophecies refer to, agree that Mark 13 is above all a warning against being led astray by people who claim to know.

a: 'I am he,'
p: The Greek says only "I am." Claimants will use Jesus' own name or authority, perhaps even God's way of speaking.
b: Matthew 24:5 spells it out: "I am the Messiah." Mark has the bare words ἐγώ εἰμι, "I am," which English has to fill out as "I am he." The same words are Jesus' own in 6:50 (walking on the water) and before the high priest in 14:62, and in the Greek Old Testament they are how God speaks of himself (Isaiah 43:10; Exodus 3:14 has a similar form). The warning may be about rival messiahs, about people who claim to be Jesus come back, or about prophets who speak as if they were God. Josephus names several men in the 40s to 60s AD who drew crowds with promises of signs (Theudas; the Egyptian, Acts 21:38).

a: This has to happen
p: "Has to happen" echoes Daniel 2:28 in the Greek: what God has set to take place.
b: The Greek δεῖ γενέσθαι, "it must happen," is the phrase the Greek translation of Daniel 2:28 uses for what God has revealed "in the last days," and Revelation 1:1 picks it up for "what must soon take place." The point is not fate but God's plan: wars do not mean God has lost control, and they do not mean the end has arrived. Matthew 24:6 keeps the same words.

a: the start of the labor pains
p: Labor pains are painful but they lead to a birth: the troubles are the beginning, not the end.
b: Prophets compared the coming of God's day to a woman in labor (Isaiah 13:8; Isaiah 26:17–18; Micah 4:9–10), and later Jewish writers spoke of the "birth pangs of the Messiah," the troubles before the age to come. Jesus uses the image both to warn and to comfort: the pains will be real, and they are only a start. Paul uses the same picture in 1 Thessalonians 5:3 and Romans 8:22. See the note at Matthew 24:8.
r: Isaiah 13:8; Isaiah 26:17–18; Micah 4:9–10; Romans 8:22; 1 Thessalonians 5:3; Matthew 24:8

a: in synagogues you will be beaten
p: Every setting named here appears in Acts and Paul's letters: local Jewish courts, synagogue floggings, Roman governors and kings.
b: "Councils" (συνέδρια) are local Jewish courts, smaller versions of the Jerusalem Sanhedrin. Synagogues could punish members with lashes; Paul says he received "forty lashes less one" five times (2 Corinthians 11:24, following the limit in Deuteronomy 25:3). Governors and kings are Roman officials and client rulers such as Felix, Festus and Agrippa, before whom Paul stood (Acts 24–26). Mark 13:9–13 is fuller than Matthew 24 here (Matthew moved most of it to his chapter 10). For Mark's first readers, whom tradition places in Rome after Nero's attack on Christians in AD 64, these were not distant predictions.
r: 2 Corinthians 11:24; Deuteronomy 25:3; Acts 5:40; Acts 24:1–27; Acts 25:1–27; Acts 26:1–32; Matthew 10:17–18; Luke 21:12–13

a: first the good news must be proclaimed to all the nations
p: Before the end, the good news must reach the nations. Many scholars hear Mark's own voice and his Gentile church here.
b: The verse breaks the flow between 13:9 and 13:11, and many scholars think Mark placed it here to tell a mostly Gentile church why the end had not yet come: the mission comes first. Some read the end of 13:9 with it: "as evidence to them and to all the nations." Readers differ on whether this was done in the first century (Paul says the message had gone "in all creation under heaven," Colossians 1:23; compare Romans 15:19) or whether it is still being done. The longer ending of Mark returns to the same command (16:15).

a: but the Holy Spirit
p: The promise to a frightened witness echoes God's promise to Moses: "I will be with your mouth."
b: Moses objected that he could not speak, and God promised to be with his mouth and teach him what to say (Exodus 4:12). Jesus gives the same help to disciples on trial. Mark names the Holy Spirit; Matthew 10:20 has "the Spirit of your Father," and Luke 21:15 has Jesus himself giving "a mouth and wisdom." In Acts, Peter speaks "filled with the Holy Spirit" before the same Sanhedrin that condemned Jesus (Acts 4:8).
r: Exodus 4:12; Matthew 10:19–20; Luke 12:11–12; Luke 21:14–15; Acts 4:8; Acts 6:10

a: One brother will hand another over to be killed
p: The Roman historian Tacitus says the Christians arrested in AD 64 named others, and "a huge crowd" followed.
b: The picture of a family turned against itself comes from Micah 7:6, which Matthew 10:35–36 quotes. Mark's readers may have known it from experience. Tacitus says that after the fire of Rome in AD 64, Nero arrested those who admitted to being Christians, "then, on their information, a huge crowd" were convicted. Mark uses the same verb "hand over" for Judas, for the priests and for Pilate (14:10; 15:1; 15:15), so the disciples' suffering follows the path of their Lord. Matthew 10:21 has the same Greek.

a: standing where he must not stand
p: Mark's Greek makes the "abomination" (a neuter noun) stand as a "he." Mark has someone in mind.
b: "Abomination" (βδέλυγμα) is neuter in Greek, but the participle "standing" (ἑστηκότα) is masculine. Matthew 24:15 smooths it to "standing in a holy place." Later copyists smoothed Mark too: the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus read the neuter ἑστώς, so the KJV has "standing where it ought not" (see the variant). Daniel's phrase (Daniel 9:27; Daniel 11:31; Daniel 12:11) first meant the pagan altar or image Antiochus IV set up in the Temple in 167 BC (1 Maccabees 1:54). Readers since have looked for the person Mark means: the emperor Gaius Caligula, who in AD 40 ordered his statue set up in the Temple and died before it was done; the Zealot leaders who seized the Temple and shed blood there in 67–68; Titus and his soldiers, who brought their standards into the court and sacrificed to them in AD 70; or a future Antichrist like the "man of lawlessness" who sits in God's temple (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4). See the views at Matthew 24:15 and the deep dive on this chapter page.
r: Daniel 9:27; Daniel 11:31; Daniel 12:11; 1 Maccabees 1:54; 2 Thessalonians 2:3–4; Matthew 24:15; Luke 21:20

a: the one who reads this should think about what it means
p: In Mark, which does not name Daniel here, the aside most naturally speaks to the reader of Mark's own book.
b: In Matthew 24:15, where Daniel is named, "the one who reads" could be a reader of Daniel. Mark's text (in the oldest manuscripts) does not mention Daniel, so most scholars take the words as Mark breaking into the speech to address whoever reads the Gospel, probably aloud to a church. The aside suggests that the meaning had to be handled carefully, perhaps because it touched Rome, and that Mark expected his readers to recognize something in their own time. That is why the verse is central to the debate over when Mark wrote.

a: in winter
p: Winter rains flooded the wadis and the Jordan. Mark, writing for Gentiles, has no "or on a Sabbath."
b: In the land of Israel the cold rains fall from about November to March. Roads turned to mud and rivers rose; Josephus tells of refugees from Gadara in the spring of AD 68 trapped by the Roman cavalry against a Jordan swollen by rain. Matthew 24:20 adds "or on a Sabbath," a worry for Jewish believers who kept the Sabbath limits on travel. Mark leaves it out, one of many signs that his readers were mostly not Jewish (compare 7:3–4, where he explains Jewish customs).

a: Nothing like it has happened from the start of the creation God made until now
p: The words follow Daniel 12:1, a time of distress such as never has been, from which God's people are rescued.
b: Daniel 12:1 promises "a time of distress" like none since nations began, in which Michael stands up for Daniel's people and "everyone found written in the book" is rescued. Mark doubles the wording about creation ("the start of the creation that God created," literally), a Semitic way of speaking. Preterist readers apply it to the siege of Jerusalem, which Josephus also called the worst disaster since the world began; futurist readers to a final great tribulation; many see a near event that foreshadows a final one. See the views at Matthew 24:21.

a: he has made the days shorter
p: Mark puts the shortening in the past tense, as already decided by God, and says "the Lord," meaning God.
b: Matthew 24:22 says the days "will be made shorter." Mark uses past tenses: "if the Lord had not shortened ... he has shortened." The tense speaks of God's decision as already made, so the readers can trust it before it happens. "The Lord" here is God the Father, as often in the Old Testament wording Mark keeps. "No one at all" is literally "all flesh," a Hebrew way of saying every human being. "The chosen" are God's people, the same word as 13:22 and 13:27.

a: false messiahs and false prophets
p: Josephus describes men who promised signs from God and drew crowds into the desert. Rome killed them and their followers.
b: In the decades before the war, Josephus tells of a Theudas who promised to part the Jordan, an Egyptian who led thousands to the Mount of Olives promising that the walls would fall, and, during the burning of the Temple in AD 70, a prophet who told people to go up into the Temple to receive "signs of deliverance." Mark warns that signs and wonders prove nothing on their own: they can be used to lead even God's chosen people astray (compare Deuteronomy 13:1–3).
r: Deuteronomy 13:1–3; 13:6; Acts 5:36; Acts 21:38; Matthew 24:24; 2 Thessalonians 2:9; Revelation 13:13

a: after that suffering
p: Matthew says "right after the suffering." Mark says only "in those days, after that suffering."
b: Matthew 24:29 begins with "immediately" (εὐθέως), which makes the time link with the suffering of 13:14–20 very tight and is the hardest word in that chapter for readers who place the coming in the future. Mark, who uses "immediately" more than any other New Testament writer, does not use it here. "In those days" is a common prophetic phrase for the time of God's action (Jeremiah 33:15; Joel 2:29; Zechariah 8:23) and can cover a span. Readers still differ on how long a gap Mark allows.

a: 'the sun will turn dark, and the moon will not shed its glow
p: The words come from Isaiah's oracles against Babylon and Edom, where a darkened sky announces the fall of an empire.
b: Mark 13:24–25 weaves together Isaiah 13:10 (Babylon: "the moon will not make its light shine") and Isaiah 34:4 (Edom: the army of heaven rots and the stars fall like leaves). Joel 2:10 and Amos 8:9 use the same pictures for the day of the LORD. In the prophets, such language described real historical judgments in cosmic terms, which is why preterist readers apply it to the fall of Jerusalem; other readers take it literally of the end of the present world, and many hold that it does both. The sky also goes dark at noon at the cross (15:33).
r: Isaiah 13:10; Isaiah 34:4; Joel 2:10; Joel 2:31; Amos 8:9; Ezekiel 32:7; 15:33; Revelation 6:12–13

a: the Son of Man coming in clouds
p: In Daniel 7 "one like a son of man" comes with the clouds to God and receives a kingdom.
b: Daniel 7:13–14 sees one "like a son of man" coming with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days, to be given rule over all peoples. Mark uses it three times: here, at 8:38, and before the high priest (14:62). Some scholars, such as N. T. Wright, read the coming as upward, to God, a vindication shown in the fall of the Temple; most Christian readers take it as Christ's return to earth. Mark's wording is "in clouds" and "with much power and glory"; Matthew 24:30 has "on the clouds of the sky." See the views at Matthew 24:30.

a: from the farthest edge of the earth to the farthest edge of the sky
p: God promised to gather scattered Israel even from "the farthest edge of the sky." Now the Son of Man sends angels to gather his chosen.
b: Deuteronomy 30:4 promises that even if Israel has been driven "to the farthest edge of the sky," God will gather them, and Zechariah 2:6 speaks of the four winds. Mark joins two expressions, "edge of the earth" and "edge of the sky," to mean everywhere at all. The striking change is the subject: in the prophets God gathers his people; here the Son of Man sends the angels and gathers "his" chosen. Matthew 24:31 adds the great trumpet of Isaiah 27:13.
r: Deuteronomy 30:4; Zechariah 2:6; Isaiah 43:5–6; Isaiah 27:13; Matthew 24:31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17

a: Learn this parable from the fig tree
p: Mark's earlier fig tree (11:12–21) was cursed for having only leaves. This one's leaves are a good sign.
b: In Palestine most trees keep their leaves through winter, but the fig loses them, so new fig leaves are a sure sign of summer. Readers of Mark have just seen another fig tree with leaves and no fruit, cursed by Jesus and withered, framing his action in the Temple (11:12–25). Many scholars take that tree as a sign of judgment on the Temple. Here the leaves mean that the events Jesus has described are close. The same tree marks both judgment and hope. The saying matches Matthew 24:32 word for word in Greek.

a: this generation will not be gone before all these things happen
p: Jesus' hearers or a later generation? Mark's readers would also remember 9:1.
b: "This generation" in Mark means Jesus' contemporaries (8:12, 38; 9:19). Readers who hold that "all these things" means the fall of the Temple say the promise was kept within forty years. Others take "these things" as the signs only, or "generation" as a race or kind of people, or see a near and a far fulfillment. Some critical scholars hold that Jesus or the early church expected the end within a lifetime. Mark's readers would have heard this beside 9:1, "some standing here will not taste death." The full range of views is at Matthew 24:34.

a: and the Son does not know
p: In Mark these words stand in nearly every manuscript. The Son does not know the day.
b: In Matthew 24:36 some important manuscripts leave out "nor the Son," probably because copyists found it hard. In Mark the words are in nearly all copies; only a few late ones lack them. This is one of the few places where Jesus calls himself simply "the Son" in Mark, set above the angels and beside the Father, and yet he says he does not know the day. Church fathers and theologians have explained it in several ways, and some groups have used it against the Son's full divinity; see the Where Christians differ card on this chapter page. Practically, the verse ends all date-setting: if the Son did not claim to know, no one else can.

a: the doorkeeper
t: A short parable of an absent master
p: Mark's version of the waiting-servant parables: every slave has a task, and the doorkeeper must not sleep.
b: Matthew and Luke have longer parables of absent masters and slaves (Matthew 24:45–51; Matthew 25:14–30; Luke 12:35–48; Luke 19:12–27). Mark's is a sketch: the master leaves, gives each slave authority and work, and tells the doorkeeper to watch. Early readers often saw church leaders in the doorkeeper; others see every believer, since 13:37 says "I tell everyone." Waiting, in this picture, is not idleness: each has a job to do while watching.

a: late in the evening, at midnight, at rooster crow, or at dawn
t: Four night watches, and one night
p: Mark uses the Roman four watches of the night. The same four times mark the night Jesus is handed over.
b: Jews often counted three watches of the night (Judges 7:19); Romans counted four, and Mark names them in popular terms: evening, midnight, cockcrow, early morning. This is one of many hints that Mark wrote for readers who lived by Roman ways. Many interpreters, among them R. H. Lightfoot, have noticed that the next chapters run through the same night: the supper "as evening fell" (14:17), Gethsemane in the dark, the rooster crowing at Peter's denial (14:72), and the handing over to Pilate "at first light" (15:1). The master came, and the disciples slept.

a: stay awake!
t: The last word of the speech, and Gethsemane
p: Jesus' last public teaching ends with "stay awake." Days later three of these four listeners fall asleep.
b: The verb γρηγορέω, "stay awake," closes the speech (13:34, 35, 37) and returns in Gethsemane, where Jesus tells Peter, James and John to "stay awake" and finds them sleeping three times (14:34, 37, 38). The Greek even repeats "find you sleeping" (13:36; 14:37, 40). Mark seems to want his readers to see the first test of watchfulness come almost at once, and fail. The warning is not only for a far future night.

a: were looking for a way to seize Jesus by a trick and kill him
p: Mark wraps the anointing (14:3–9) between the plot (14:1–2) and Judas's offer (14:10–11). Each part explains the other.
b: Mark often splits one story and puts another inside it, a "sandwich" (3:20–35; 5:21–43; 6:7–30; 11:12–25; 14:54–72). Here the outer layers are the plot against Jesus; the inner story is a woman who pours out costly oil in love. The contrast is the point: the leaders plot in secret, a disciple sells his teacher for money, and an unnamed woman gives away a year's wages and prepares Jesus for his burial. Matthew keeps the frame; Luke and John place the anointing elsewhere.

a: Not at the festival
t: "Not at the festival" or "not in the festival crowd"
p: The leaders may mean "not during the feast" or "not among the festival crowds." Either way, it happens at the feast.
b: The Greek ἐν τῇ ἑορτῇ usually means "during the festival." Joachim Jeremias argued that ἑορτή can also mean the festival gathering, so the leaders mean "not in front of the festival crowd," which fits the arrest at night away from the city. On the usual reading their plan fails, and Jesus dies at Passover after all; on Jeremias's reading, their plan works through Judas. See also the note on the festival riot at Matthew 26:5.

a: real nard that cost a great deal
p: Nard was an oil from a plant of the Himalayas, carried to Rome by long trade routes. "Real" is uncertain.
b: Spikenard comes from a plant that grows in the high Himalayas, and its oil reached the Mediterranean through India at great cost. The word translated "real" (πιστικῆς) is rare and debated. Most take it from πιστός, "faithful, genuine," so "real, unmixed" nard; others suggest a word for the pistachio tree, or a place name. John 12:3 uses the same unusual phrase, one of the links between the two accounts, and the Plain gives it the same English there.
r: John 12:3; Song of Songs 1:12; Song of Songs 4:13–14

a: She broke the jar open and poured the oil over his head
p: Prophets poured oil on the heads of kings. "Messiah" means "anointed one." The woman anoints the King for his burial.
b: Samuel poured oil on Saul's head (1 Samuel 10:1), and a prophet's disciple poured it on Jehu's (2 Kings 9:6). "Messiah" and "Christ" both mean "anointed." In Mark, no priest or prophet anoints Jesus as king; an unnamed woman does, two days before he is mocked as "King of the Jews" and crucified. Breaking the jar means the whole of it was used. Jesus himself gives the act a second meaning, burial (14:8). On the anointing in John and Luke, see the note on 14:4 and the topic page.

a: Some of those there grew angry
t: Who complained? Three anointings or one?
p: Mark says "some," Matthew "the disciples," John "Judas." Luke tells a different anointing in Galilee.
b: Mark leaves the complainers unnamed; Matthew 26:8 says the disciples; John 12:4–6 names Judas and calls him a thief. John also names the woman (Mary of Bethany), places the meal six days before Passover, and has her anoint Jesus' feet. Luke 7:36–50 tells of a sinful woman who anoints his feet in a Pharisee's house in Galilee. Many scholars think Mark/Matthew and John tell the same event, and Luke a separate one; others think all three go back to one memory told differently. Later Western tradition merged the women with Mary Magdalene, which the Gospels do not say.

a: three hundred denarii
p: A denarius was a laborer's pay for a day. Three hundred was close to a year's work, after Sabbaths and feasts.
b: Matthew 20:2 shows a denarius as the day's wage of a field worker. A man who worked six days a week, minus festivals, might earn about three hundred in a year. The oil cost what a poor family lived on for a year, and the woman poured it out at once. Among the first three Gospels only Mark gives the figure; John 12:5 has it too. The complaint was not foolish: giving alms to the poor was a duty, especially at Passover.

a: they turned on her angrily
p: The verb means to snort like a horse: an angry, scolding reaction.
b: The verb ἐμβριμάομαι is used in Greek of horses snorting, and in the New Testament of strong, angry feeling. Mark used it of Jesus sternly sending away the man healed of skin disease (1:43), and John of Jesus' deep anger at Lazarus's tomb (John 11:33, 38). Here it shows how harshly the others scolded the woman, and makes Jesus' "Leave her alone" a real defense.

a: you are able to help them whenever you wish
p: Jesus is not shrugging at poverty. He alludes to Deuteronomy 15:11, a command to open your hand.
b: Deuteronomy 15:11 says, "For there will never stop being people in need in the land. That is why I am commanding you: Open your hand wide." Jesus' hearers knew the rest of the verse. Mark alone adds "you are able to help them whenever you wish," which keeps the duty in view: the poor will always be there to help, but Jesus is about to die. The saying is about this moment, not a rule that poverty does not matter. See the note at Matthew 26:11.

a: She has come ahead of time to put oil on my body for its burial
t: The burial anointing that came first
p: After Jesus dies, women come to anoint his body and cannot (16:1–6). This woman has already done it.
b: Jesus will be buried in haste before the Sabbath, and Mark mentions no anointing (15:46). On Sunday the women bring spices to anoint him, but he is no longer there (16:1–6). Mark seems to have set the two scenes to answer each other: the only anointing Jesus' body receives is this one, given in advance by a woman who understood, or acted as if she understood, what the disciples would not accept (8:31–33). "She has done what was in her power" is literally "what she had, she did."

a: so that she is remembered
p: Jesus says her deed will be told wherever the good news goes. Mark never gives her name.
b: This is the only time in Mark that Jesus promises someone will be remembered in the preaching of the good news. Yet the woman stays nameless, while Judas, in the next verse, is named. Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza took the title of her landmark feminist study, In Memory of Her (1983), from this verse, arguing that the church kept the betrayer's name and lost the faithful woman's. Others note that Mark leaves many faithful people unnamed, and that John 12:3 names her as Mary of Bethany.

a: Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve
p: Mark gives no reason why Judas went. Matthew suggests money, Luke and John Satan.
b: The Greek says "the one of the Twelve," an odd phrase that stresses he was one of the inner circle (3:19 named him already as the one who would hand Jesus over). Mark does not explain him. Matthew 26:15 has Judas ask what they will pay; Luke 22:3 and John 13:27 say Satan entered him; John 12:6 calls him a thief. Modern guesses (disappointed nationalism, an attempt to force Jesus to act) go beyond the texts. Mark's silence keeps the reader's eyes on the frightening fact itself: one of the Twelve.

a: when the Passover lambs were sacrificed
p: Mark makes the Last Supper a Passover meal. John puts Jesus' death on the day the lambs were killed.
b: The lambs were slaughtered at the Temple on the afternoon of 14 Nisan and eaten that evening, which by Jewish reckoning was 15 Nisan. Strictly, the Feast of Unleavened Bread began on the 15th, but the 14th, when leaven was removed, was often counted as its first day (Josephus does so). In Mark the supper is the Passover meal; in John 18:28 and 19:14 Jesus dies on the afternoon the lambs were killed. Scholars explain the difference by different calendars, by John's theology of Jesus as the Lamb, or by Mark's. Matthew 26:17 has the full discussion.
r: Exodus 12:6; Deuteronomy 16:1–8; Matthew 26:17; Luke 22:7; John 18:28; John 19:14; 1 Corinthians 5:7

a: a man carrying a clay jar of water
p: Women usually carried water jars. A man doing it would stand out: a signal, arranged or foreseen.
b: In the ancient Near East, fetching water in jars was usually women's work (Genesis 24:11; John 4:7); men more often carried water in skins. A man with a jar would be easy to spot. Some take it as a plan made ahead to keep the meeting place secret from the authorities (and from Judas); others see Jesus' foreknowledge, as in the finding of the colt (11:2–6). The two scenes are told in almost the same words.

a: a big room upstairs
p: A large upstairs room with dining couches. Tradition links it with the house of Mark's mother, but the Gospels do not say so.
b: Wealthier houses in Jerusalem had large upper rooms; "laid out" (ἐστρωμένον) means spread with couches or rugs for reclining at a festive meal. Acts 1:13 places the disciples in an upper room after Easter, and Acts 12:12 mentions the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, where believers met. Some later writers joined these and guessed that the supper was in Mark's family house, and even that Mark was the man with the jar or the young man of 14:51. These are guesses, not evidence. The present "Cenacle" on Mount Zion is a Crusader-era building.

a: a man eating with me
t: The friend who ate my bread
p: Jesus' words echo Psalm 41:9, where the betrayer is a friend who shared a meal.
b: Psalm 41:9 laments a trusted friend "who ate my bread" and turned against the writer. John 13:18 quotes the psalm outright; Mark only hints at it. Eating together created a bond of loyalty in the ancient world, so the betrayal is worse because it comes from someone at the table. "As they lay at the table": at a festive meal, and at Passover above all, people reclined on couches, leaning on the left elbow, as free people did (Mishnah Pesachim 10:1).

a: just as it stands written about him
p: No single verse says the Son of Man must be handed over. Mark probably means the whole pattern of Scripture.
b: Mark often says the Son of Man must suffer "as it is written" (9:12; 14:49), without quoting one text. Readers point to the suffering servant of Isaiah 53, the righteous sufferer of Psalms 22, 41 and 69, the struck shepherd of Zechariah 13:7 (quoted at 14:27), and the son of man of Daniel 7, who first appears with the saints who are crushed before they are given the kingdom. Jesus holds both God's plan and Judas's guilt together: it is written, and it is still "woe" to the one who does it. See the note on free will at Matthew 26:24.

a: This is my body
t: Mark's short words over the bread
p: Mark's form is the shortest in the New Testament: "Take it. This is my body." How Christians understand it is shown at Matthew 26.
b: Matthew adds "and eat"; Paul and Luke add "which is for you" (or "given for you") and "do this in remembrance of me" (1 Corinthians 11:24; Luke 22:19). Joachim Jeremias argued that Mark's wording, with its Semitic turns of phrase, is close to the oldest form, though Paul's letter is the oldest written account. If Jesus spoke Aramaic, his sentence probably had no word for "is" at all, yet much later debate turns on what "is" means: the deep dive on the Last Supper and the Where Christians differ cards at Matthew 26:26–28 set out the Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican, Methodist and Baptist views.

a: every one of them drank from it
t: The cup they said they could drink
p: James and John had said, "We can" drink Jesus' cup (10:38–39). Now all drink, and within hours all run away.
b: In Matthew 26:27 Jesus commands, "Every one of you, drink from it." Mark simply reports that all drank, and only then gives the words over the cup. Mark's readers had heard Jesus ask James and John whether they could drink the cup he would drink (10:38). The word "all" runs through the night: all drink (14:23), all will be tripped up (14:27), all promise not to deny him (14:31), all abandon him (14:50).

a: my blood of the covenant
p: At Sinai Moses splashed blood on the people: "Here is the blood of the covenant." Jesus speaks of his own blood.
b: Moses sealed the covenant at Sinai by sacrifice: "Here is the blood of the covenant" (Exodus 24:8). Zechariah 9:11 speaks of "the blood of your covenant" as the reason for setting prisoners free. Jeremiah 31:31 promised a new covenant, and Paul and Luke say "the new covenant in my blood" (1 Corinthians 11:25; Luke 22:20). In Mark's oldest manuscripts the word "new" is not there (see the variant), but the meaning is close: Jesus' death founds God's covenant people.
r: Exodus 24:8; Zechariah 9:11; Jeremiah 31:31–34; Hebrews 9:18–22; Matthew 26:28; 1 Corinthians 11:25

a: It is being poured out for many
p: "Many" echoes the servant of Isaiah 53, who "bore the sin of many," and Jesus' own word about a ransom (10:45).
b: Isaiah 53:12 ends the song of the suffering servant: "He bore the sin of many." Jesus had said that the Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45). In Hebrew idiom "the many" can mean the whole community, not "many but not all." Matthew 26:28 adds "so that sins can be forgiven"; Mark leaves the cup word without it.

a: until that day, the day I drink it new in the kingdom of God
p: Jesus vows not to drink wine again until God's kingdom comes. The meal points ahead to the feast of the age to come.
b: Many scholars hear a solemn vow of abstinence, the kind Israelites took in a crisis. It also looks ahead. Isaiah 25:6–8 promises a feast of "aged wine" on God's mountain when death is swallowed up, and Jesus had spoken of many coming to eat in the kingdom (Matthew 8:11). Every later celebration of the Supper keeps this hope: Paul says it proclaims the Lord's death "until he comes" (1 Corinthians 11:26). Matthew 26:29 adds "with you" and "my Father's" kingdom.

a: I will get to Galilee ahead of you
t: A promise kept for the end
p: The promise returns in the last words spoken in the oldest form of Mark: "He is going on ahead of you to Galilee" (16:7).
b: Right after predicting that all will scatter, Jesus promises to regather them like a shepherd going ahead of his flock. The young man at the tomb repeats it almost word for word: "He is going on ahead of you to Galilee ... as he told you" (16:7). In a Gospel that ends at 16:8, this promise is the reader's assurance that the scattered disciples will be restored, even though Mark does not narrate it. Willi Marxsen and Ernst Lohmeyer argued that Galilee also stands for the place of mission among the nations.

a: today, this very night
p: A Jewish day began at sunset. The evening of the supper was already "today" in the reckoning of the day Jesus died.
b: Jews counted days from sunset to sunset (Genesis 1:5 "evening and morning"). So the supper, the arrest, the trials, the crucifixion and the burial all fall on one Jewish day. Mark piles up the time words, "today, this very night," and adds "you yourself" (σύ), to make the prediction sharp against Peter's boast. Only Mark has the rooster crowing twice; see the variant and the note at 14:72.
orig: σὺ σήμερον ταύτῃ τῇ νυκτί (sy sēmeron tautē tē nykti)

a: deeply alarmed and distressed
t: Alarm in the garden and at the tomb
p: Mark uses a strong word for shock and alarm only of Jesus here and of the women at the empty tomb (16:5–6).
b: The verb ἐκθαμβέομαι, "be utterly amazed, alarmed," is found in the New Testament only in Mark: of the crowd seeing Jesus after the transfiguration (9:15), of Jesus in Gethsemane, and of the women at the tomb, where the young man says, "Do not be alarmed" (16:5–6). The second verb, ἀδημονέω, means anguish or deep distress. Mark does not soften Jesus' horror at what is coming; Luke 22:44 shows it in sweat like drops of blood. Church fathers used verses like this to show that Jesus had a true human soul and feelings.

a: My soul is crushed with grief
t: The psalm of a downcast soul
p: Jesus speaks in the words of Psalms 42–43: "Why are you so bowed down, my soul?"
b: The Greek word for "crushed with grief" (περίλυπος) is the word the Greek Psalms use in the refrain of Psalms 42–43: "Why are you so bowed down, my soul?" (Psalm 42:5). That psalm goes on, "Wait for God, for I will thank him again." "Enough to kill me" (literally "to death") may echo Jonah 4:9 or Sirach 37:2, a grief that kills. Matthew 26:38 has the same words.
r: Psalm 42:5; Psalm 42:11; Psalm 43:5; Jonah 4:9; Matthew 26:38; John 12:27

a: Abba, Father
p: Abba is Aramaic for "father." It was a family word, but it does not mean "Daddy," as is often said.
b: Mark keeps the Aramaic word Jesus used and translates it for Greek readers: "Abba, Father." Paul shows that Greek-speaking Christians kept the word in prayer (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6). Joachim Jeremias argued that no Jew of the time addressed God as Abba in prayer and that it was a child's word, like "Daddy." James Barr showed in 1988 that adult children also used abba and that it is not baby talk, and others have found Jewish prayers calling God "Father." What stands out is the trust: Jesus asks to be spared and then yields to his Father's will.
orig: Αββα ὁ πατήρ (abba ho patēr); Aramaic אבא, 'father'

a: Make this cup pass me by
p: In the prophets the cup is God's wrath that the nations must drink. Jesus has spoken of his cup before (10:38).
b: "The cup" in the prophets is often the cup of God's anger (Isaiah 51:17, 22; Jeremiah 25:15; Psalm 75:8). Jesus asked James and John whether they could drink his cup (10:38), and he has just given his disciples a cup of the covenant in his blood (14:23–24). Here he shrinks from drinking it. Readers have seen in the cup his suffering and death, or the judgment he bears for others. See the note at Matthew 26:39.
r: Isaiah 51:17; Isaiah 51:22; Jeremiah 25:15; Psalm 75:8; 10:38; Matthew 26:39; John 18:11

a: Simon, are you sleeping?
p: For the first time since 3:16 Jesus calls Peter by his old name, Simon. The Rock is asleep.
b: Jesus gave Simon the name Peter, "Rock," in 3:16, and Mark calls him Peter from then on. Here, alone, Jesus addresses him as "Simon." Many readers take it as a quiet rebuke: he is not living up to his new name. Peter had just said he would never deny Jesus; now he cannot keep awake for one hour. Mark is often said to be the Gospel most influenced by Peter (Papias), and also the one hardest on him.

a: They had no idea how to answer him
p: The same three disciples, the same sleepiness, the same loss for words as at the transfiguration (9:6).
b: At the transfiguration Peter did not know what to answer (9:6), and Luke adds that the three were heavy with sleep (Luke 9:32). Mark uses almost the same words here. On the mountain the three saw Jesus' glory; in the garden they see his anguish. Both times they fail to understand. The parallel invites readers to hold the glory and the suffering together.

a: It is enough.
p: The one Greek word apechei is one of the hardest in Mark. "It is enough" is the most common guess.
b: The verb ἀπέχει can mean "it is enough," "it is far away," or, in the language of business receipts, "he has received (payment)." So readers suggest: "Enough sleeping!"; "Has the end come? No, it is still far off," said in irony; or "He (Judas) has been paid," since 14:11 mentions money. Codex Bezae and some other witnesses add "the end" (ἀπέχει τὸ τέλος), a phrase whose sense is itself debated: "the end has come" (compare Luke 22:37, where τέλος ἔχει is used of what is written about Jesus) or "the end is settled." Whatever it means, Jesus' next words are clear: the hour has come.

a: he kissed him
p: Judas's sign is the ordinary greeting of a disciple to a teacher. The verb is stronger than in 14:44.
b: In 14:44 Judas says "whoever I kiss" with the plain verb φιλέω; here Mark uses the compound καταφιλέω. Some take it as "kissed him warmly" or "kissed him again and again," which makes the betrayal colder; others note that the compound was often used without extra force. A kiss was how a disciple greeted his rabbi, so the sign would mark Jesus out in the dark without raising alarm. See the note at Matthew 26:49.

a: someone among those standing by
p: Mark does not say it was a disciple. John names Peter, and the slave Malchus.
b: Mark's wording is vague: "a certain one of those standing by." Matthew 26:51 says it was one of those with Jesus, and Luke 22:50–51 adds that Jesus healed the ear. John 18:10 names Peter and the slave, Malchus. Some think Mark (and the earliest tellers) kept the name quiet while Peter was alive and could be prosecuted; others think the name was added later. Mark gives no word from Jesus about the sword, unlike Matthew 26:52.

a: Then they all abandoned him and ran off
p: The disciples who had left everything to follow him now leave him. The scattering of 14:27 has come true.
b: At their call the first disciples "left" their nets and their father to follow Jesus (1:18, 20; the same verb ἀφίημι). Now they "left" him. Jesus had quoted Zechariah 13:7: the shepherd struck, the sheep scattered (14:27). From here Jesus is alone in Mark until his death. Only the women watching from a distance remain (15:40–41).

a: A certain young man
p: Only Mark tells of him. Readers have seen Mark himself, a symbol of the fleeing disciples, or a hint of the young man at the tomb.
b: The story has no purpose in the plot, which is why many readers think it must mean something. Views: (1) Mark's signature, an eyewitness memory of his own (a popular guess since the 1800s, with no ancient support). (2) A picture of discipleship failing: the disciples had left everything to follow; this follower leaves even his clothes to get away. (3) A fulfillment of Amos 2:16, where the bravest soldier flees naked on that day. (4) A link to the "young man" (the same word, νεανίσκος) in a white robe at the tomb (16:5): one flees naked in a linen cloth, the other sits clothed in white, and some see a picture of baptism, death and new life. (5) Simply a vivid memory.

a: he left the cloth in their hands and fled naked
t: The linen cloth and Secret Mark
p: A letter reported in 1958 quotes a "secret" Mark with another young man in linen. Many think it a modern forgery.
b: "Linen cloth" (σινδών) is the same word as Jesus' burial cloth (15:46). In 1958 Morton Smith reported finding, at the Mar Saba monastery, a copy of a letter said to be by Clement of Alexandria (about AD 200). It quotes a longer "Secret Gospel of Mark" with a story of a rich young man raised from the dead who comes to Jesus at night wearing a linen cloth over his naked body. The pages are now lost; Smith's black-and-white photographs and colour photographs taken in 1977 survive. The Secret Gospel of Mark is in no church's Bible. Scholars divide sharply: Stephen Carlson (2005) and Peter Jeffery (2007) argue that Smith forged it; Scott Brown (2005) and others defend it as an ancient letter. See the deep dive on this chapter page.

a: warming himself at the fire's light
p: Mark sandwiches Jesus' trial (14:55–65) inside Peter's denial (14:54, 66–72). Jesus confesses; Peter denies.
b: Mark places Peter by the fire, cuts to Jesus before the council, and returns to Peter below in the courtyard. The two scenes happen at the same time and comment on each other. Upstairs Jesus stays silent before false witnesses and then openly says "I am"; downstairs Peter speaks only to deny. Upstairs they mock Jesus with "Be a prophet!" (14:65), while downstairs his prophecy about Peter comes true. "The fire's light" is literally "the light": Peter can be seen.

a: the whole Sanhedrin
p: Later Jewish law forbade capital trials at night or on a feast. Whether those rules applied in AD 30 is debated.
b: The Sanhedrin was Jerusalem's council of priests, elders and scribes under the high priest. The Mishnah (written down about AD 200) says capital cases must be tried by day, not on the eve of a Sabbath or feast, and need a second session for a guilty verdict (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:1). Mark's night hearing breaks these rules. Scholars answer that the Mishnah may describe ideals of a later age, that Sadducee priests followed other rules, that this was a hearing to prepare a charge for Pilate (15:1), or that Mark has shaped the scene. The full discussion is in the deep dive at Matthew 26.

a: their testimonies did not match
p: The Law required two or three witnesses. Mark stresses that theirs did not agree, so by the Law's own test the case failed.
b: Deuteronomy 17:6 and 19:15 require at least two witnesses for a death sentence, and Jewish practice examined witnesses separately to see whether they agreed. The story of Susanna, in the Greek additions to Daniel, turns on exactly this: two elders are exposed when their testimony does not match. Mark says twice that the testimony did not agree (14:56, 59). The verdict will come instead from Jesus' own answer.

a: this sanctuary that human hands made
p: "Made by hands" is the Greek Bible's word for idols. The charge is false, but Mark's readers know a true sense in it.
b: In the Greek Old Testament, χειροποίητος, "handmade," describes idols (Leviticus 26:1; Isaiah 46:6). Stephen and Paul say God does not live in handmade temples (Acts 7:48; Acts 17:24), and Hebrews 9:11, 24 contrasts the handmade sanctuary with the true one. Mark calls the testimony false, but the charge returns at the cross (15:29), and at Jesus' death the sanctuary curtain is torn (15:38). John 2:19–21 has Jesus say "Destroy this sanctuary" and explains he meant his body.
r: 15:29; 15:38; John 2:19–21; Acts 7:48; Acts 17:24; Hebrews 9:11; Hebrews 9:24; 2 Corinthians 5:1; Matthew 26:61

a: "Are you the Messiah," he asked, "the Son of the Blessed One?"
p: Through the whole Gospel Jesus has kept his identity quiet. Now the high priest asks him outright, and he answers.
b: "The Blessed One" is a Jewish way of naming God without saying the name, as in the synagogue call to "bless the LORD, the Blessed One" (Mishnah Berakhot 7:3). Since 1901, when William Wrede named it the "messianic secret," scholars have discussed why Jesus in Mark silences demons and disciples (1:34; 8:30; 9:9). Here the secret ends: before the council, with nothing to gain and his life at stake, Jesus answers openly. Mark seems to say that he can only be known as Messiah when he is seen as the one who suffers.

a: sitting at the Power's right hand and coming with the clouds of the sky
p: Jesus joins two texts: the king who sits at God's right hand, and the son of man who comes with the clouds.
b: Psalm 110:1, "Sit at my right hand," was the text Jesus had just used to puzzle the scribes about David's son (12:35–37). Daniel 7:13 gives the one like a son of man coming with the clouds. "The Power" is a reverent way of saying God. The claim to share God's throne, and the warning that his judges will see it, is what the high priest calls blasphemy. Some read the coming as Jesus' going to God in vindication, others as his return; see the notes at 13:26 and Matthew 26:64.

a: The high priest ripped his tunics
p: Tearing one's clothes was a sign of grief or horror. Later law required judges who heard blasphemy to tear their garments.
b: People tore their clothes at news of death or disaster (Genesis 37:34; 2 Samuel 1:11), and on hearing words against God (2 Kings 18:37; 19:1). The Mishnah says that when witnesses repeat a blasphemy in court, the judges stand and tear their clothes and never sew them up (Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:5). Leviticus 21:10 forbade the high priest to tear his garments in mourning; this is a judge's act, not mourning. "Tunics" is plural: a wealthy man wore more than one. The verb is διαρρήγνυμι, "rip apart." Matthew 26:65 has the same verb, and its Plain says "tore his clothes"; the Plain of Mark says "ripped" so that "torn" stays with σχίζω, the verb of the torn heavens (1:10) and the torn curtain (15:38).

a: You heard the blasphemy.
t: Was it blasphemy under Jewish law?
p: The Mishnah defines blasphemy as speaking God's own name. Jesus did not. Scholars debate what the charge was.
b: Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:5 says a blasphemer is guilty only if he pronounces the divine name. Jesus said "the Power," not the name. Some answer that the Mishnah's narrow rule is later; others that the high priest judged the claim itself, to sit beside God on his throne, as an insult to God's honor; others that the issue for the priests was political, a messianic claimant in Passover week. Jewish historians such as Geza Vermes and Paula Fredriksen stress that the Gospels tell the story from the side of Jesus' followers and that the leaders were a small priestly group working with Rome, not the Jewish people.

a: "Be a prophet!"
t: Mocked as a prophet while his prophecy comes true
p: They cover his face and dare him to prophesy. At the same moment, in the courtyard below, his prophecy about Peter is being fulfilled.
b: Covering the face and striking is a cruel game, which Matthew spells out: "Be a prophet for us, Messiah! Who struck you?" (Matthew 26:68; compare Luke 22:64). Mark's shorter "Be a prophet!" sets up the irony of the next scene: Jesus had foretold that Peter would deny him three times before the rooster crowed twice, and it happens while they mock (14:66–72). The spitting and slapping echo the servant of Isaiah 50:6, who did not hide his face "against insult and spit."

a: the Nazarene
p: Mark always uses the form Nazarēnos, "the man from Nazareth." In the slave girl's mouth it sounds like a sneer.
b: Mark calls Jesus Ναζαρηνός, "Nazarene" (1:24; 10:47; 14:67; 16:6), where Matthew, John and Acts usually have Ναζωραῖος. Both mean a man from Nazareth, an unimportant village (John 1:46). Here the girl uses it of Jesus with contempt; at the tomb the young man uses the same word with honor: "Jesus the Nazarene, the one who was crucified" (16:6).

a: to curse and to swear
p: The Greek gives no object. Peter may call down a curse on himself if he is lying, or he may curse Jesus.
b: The verb ἀναθεματίζω means "to call down a curse," and Mark gives no object. Most translations understand a curse on himself: "may God punish me if I know him." Some scholars argue that Peter cursed Jesus, which would make the denial complete. About AD 112 the Roman governor Pliny wrote that he tested people accused of being Christians by making them curse Christ, which genuine Christians, he said, could not be forced to do. If Mark's readers faced such tests, Peter's failure, and his tears, spoke to them directly.

a: And he burst into tears
p: The word before "he wept" is unclear. It may mean he broke down, threw himself down, thought about it, or covered his head.
b: Mark says ἐπιβαλὼν ἔκλαιεν. The participle comes from a verb that means "throw on, put on." Suggestions: "he threw himself down and wept"; "he thought of it and wept" (with "his mind" understood); "he covered his head and wept"; or simply "he began to weep" or "burst into tears." Matthew 26:75 and Luke 22:62 replace it with "he went outside and cried bitterly." Peter's tears, unlike Judas's end, leave the way open for the message to "his disciples, and Peter" (16:7).

a: handed him over to Pilate
p: The verb "hand over" (paradidōmi) runs through Mark's passion: Judas, the priests, Pilate, and in the background God.
b: John the Baptist was "handed over" (1:14). Jesus three times foretold that the Son of Man would be handed over (9:31; 10:33). Now it happens in a chain: Judas hands him to the priests (14:10, 44), the priests hand him to Pilate (15:1, 10), Pilate hands him to be crucified (15:15). Jesus warned that his followers would be handed over too (13:9–12). Paul uses the same verb for God, who "handed him over for us all" (Romans 8:32), and for Jesus, who "handed himself over" (Galatians 2:20). One verb holds human betrayal and divine purpose together.

a: At first light
p: Roman officials heard cases at dawn. The council's morning decision turned a religious charge into a political one for Pilate.
b: Roman magistrates began their public business at first light and were often finished by late morning. The council therefore had to act early. Mark's "reached a decision" (literally "made a consultation") may describe a second meeting or the end of the night session. Pilate, the prefect of Judea from AD 26 to 36, normally lived at Caesarea and came to Jerusalem with troops for the great feasts. For Pilate's career and character see the note at Matthew 27:2.

a: So you are the King of the Jews?
t: "King of the Jews": a Roman charge
p: Pilate's first question is political. "King of the Jews" is how outsiders spoke; Jews said "King of Israel" (15:32).
b: Before the council the question was whether he was the Messiah, the Son of the Blessed One (14:61). Before Pilate it becomes "King of the Jews," a title Rome had given Herod the Great, and a claim no one could make without Rome's permission. The phrase appears five times in this chapter (15:2, 9, 12, 18, 26) and is turned into "King of Israel" by the priests (15:32). Mark's readers know the irony: Jesus really is the king, and his throne is a cross. See Matthew 27:11.

a: But Jesus answered nothing more
p: Jesus' silence before his judges recalls the servant of Isaiah 53, who "did not open his mouth."
b: Jesus was silent before the false witnesses (14:61) and is silent again before Pilate, speaking only the words "You are the one saying it." Isaiah 53:7 says of the servant, "yet he did not open his mouth. Like a lamb that is taken off to slaughter." Pilate's surprise suggests that accused men normally fought hard for their lives. Mark does not quote Isaiah here, but readers from Acts 8:32–35 on have heard it.

a: At the festival he used to set one prisoner free for them
p: No source outside the Gospels mentions this custom. Historians are divided on how much to make of that.
b: Mark, Matthew and John all mention a custom of releasing a prisoner at Passover (John 18:39), but no Roman or Jewish writer describes it. The Mishnah mentions a Passover lamb slaughtered for someone who has been promised release from prison (Mishnah Pesachim 8:6), which some take as indirect support. Governors did sometimes free prisoners to win goodwill. Some scholars doubt the custom and think the Barabbas scene was shaped by early Christian reflection; others accept a local practice that left no other record. See Matthew 27:15.

a: the uprising
p: Mark says "the" uprising, as if his readers knew it. No other source names it.
b: Barabbas was held with "rebels" (στασιασταί) who had committed murder "in the uprising." The article suggests a known event, perhaps a riot in Jerusalem shortly before. Josephus records several clashes under Pilate, including protests over the army's standards and over the use of Temple money for an aqueduct, but none that can be matched to this one. The name Barabbas is Aramaic, "son of the father" or "son of Abba"; in some manuscripts of Matthew he is "Jesus Barabbas" (see the variant at Matthew 27:16). The two men crucified with Jesus are called "bandits" (15:27), the word Josephus uses for rebels.

a: worked the crowd up
p: In Mark the chief priests stir up a crowd that has come to ask for a release. Mark never says "all the people."
b: The crowd that "went up" to Pilate (15:8) had come to ask for the usual release; the priests turned it toward Barabbas. Mark does not say this crowd was the same as the people who welcomed Jesus or heard him gladly (11:8–10; 12:37), and he has no line like Matthew 27:25, "His blood on us, and on our children." A few hundred people in a courtyard were not the Jewish nation. The deep dives at Matthew 27 trace how these scenes were later used against Jews, and the churches' later repudiation of that use.

a: They shouted back
p: The Greek says they shouted "again," though Mark has not reported an earlier shout. It may mean "in reply."
b: Mark writes οἱ δὲ πάλιν ἔκραξαν, literally "and they again shouted." Since no shout has been reported, some take πάλιν in the sense "back, in return," which it can have; others think Mark assumes the crowd had already been shouting for Barabbas (15:11). Either way the cry is the same word, "Crucify him!", and in 15:14 it grows louder.

a: Pilate wished to keep the crowd happy
p: Mark's Greek here copies a Latin phrase, satisfacere, "to satisfy." His Gospel has more Latin words than any other.
b: "To do what is enough" (τὸ ἱκανὸν ποιῆσαι) is a Latin turn of phrase in Greek dress. The same chapter has "whipped" (φραγελλόω, from flagellum), "Praetorium" (15:16), "cohort" (15:16), and "centurion" (κεντυρίων, 15:39, where Matthew and Luke use a Greek word). Elsewhere Mark explains Greek coins by Roman ones (12:42). Many scholars take these as signs that Mark wrote in or for a Latin-speaking setting, most likely Rome, as early tradition says; others note that Latin army and legal words were used across the eastern empire too.

a: that is, the Praetorium
p: The governor's headquarters in Jerusalem, probably Herod's palace. A cohort was a unit of several hundred soldiers.
b: Mark explains the courtyard as "the Praetorium," the Latin word for a commander's headquarters. In Jerusalem this was most likely Herod's former palace on the western hill, where governors stayed; older tradition placed it in the Antonia fortress by the Temple. A cohort (σπεῖρα) was nominally 600 men, though Mark means the soldiers on hand. These were not Romans from Italy but auxiliary troops recruited mostly from non-Jewish towns of the region, such as Caesarea and Sebaste. See Matthew 27:27.

a: They dressed him in purple
p: Soldiers mocking a prisoner as a king is a known ancient game. Philo describes a similar mock coronation in Alexandria.
b: Purple was the color of kings and emperors; a soldier's faded red cloak would do for the joke (Matthew 27:28 says "scarlet"). The crown of thorns imitates the wreath on an emperor's head on coins, and "Hail, King of the Jews!" copies the salute "Hail, Caesar!" Philo tells how a crowd in Alexandria in AD 38 dressed a harmless madman named Carabas as a king, with a papyrus crown and a reed scepter, to mock the Jewish king Agrippa. Mark's readers knew the joke was on the soldiers.

a: bowed down before him
p: The verb proskyneō means to bow down, and also to worship. The soldiers do in mockery what Mark's readers do in faith.
b: The Gospels use προσκυνέω for kneeling or bowing before someone, a gesture given to kings and to God; this site renders it "bow down" and leaves readers to see who deserves it. In Mark the word appears only twice: the man from the tombs bows before Jesus (5:6), and here soldiers kneel in mockery. In Matthew the women and the eleven bow down before the risen Jesus (Matthew 28:9, 17). Mark's readers, who honored Jesus as Lord and God's Son, would feel the irony of a mock worship that told the truth.

a: Simon of Cyrene, the father of Alexander and Rufus
p: Mark names Simon's sons as if his readers knew them. Paul greets a Rufus in Rome.
b: Cyrene, in today's Libya, had a large Jewish community, and Cyrenian Jews had a synagogue in Jerusalem (Acts 6:9). Mark alone names Simon's sons, which suggests they were known to his readers. Paul greets "Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother" in Rome (Romans 16:13), and many scholars think it may be the same man, which would fit a Roman setting for Mark. In 1941 a family tomb in the Kidron Valley was found with ossuaries of Jews from Cyrene; one is inscribed "Alexander son of Simon" (published by Nahman Avigad in 1962). The names were common, so the link is possible, not proven. "Coming in from the fields" (literally "from a field") has been used to argue that this was not yet a feast day, but it may mean only that he was entering the city.
r: Romans 16:13; Acts 6:9; Acts 11:20; Acts 13:1; Matthew 27:32; Luke 23:26

a: myrrh-flavored wine
p: Wine spiced with myrrh may have been meant to dull pain, or simply to honor. Jesus refuses it.
b: The Talmud says that women of Jerusalem gave a condemned man a cup of wine with frankincense to numb him, following Proverbs 31:6, "Give beer to someone who is perishing." Myrrh-flavored wine was a fine drink in the Roman world, so some take it as a gesture of honor or of mockery. Mark's imperfect "they kept trying to give" suggests they offered more than once. Jesus will not drink, perhaps keeping the vow of 14:25. Matthew 27:34 has "wine mixed with gall," closer to Psalm 69:21.

a: throwing lots for them
t: Psalm 22 at the foot of the cross
p: Mark tells it without a quotation, in words that echo Psalm 22:18: "over my clothing they throw lots."
b: Executioners took the clothes of the condemned. Mark's wording follows the Greek of Psalm 22:18: "They hand out my clothes among them, and over my clothing they throw lots." Psalm 22 runs through Mark's account: the passers-by who shake their heads (15:29; Psalm 22:7) and the cry "My God, my God" (15:34; Psalm 22:1). John 19:24 quotes the verse outright. On how many of these details are memory and how many were shaped by the psalm, scholars differ.

a: It was the third hour
t: The third hour and John's sixth hour
p: Mark has the crucifixion at about 9 a.m. John 19:14 has Jesus still before Pilate "about the sixth hour," about noon.
b: Mark marks the day in three-hour steps: dawn (15:1), the third hour (15:25), the sixth (15:33), the ninth (15:34), evening (15:42). John 19:14 says Pilate presented Jesus about the sixth hour. Proposed answers: (1) a copying error, since the Greek numerals for 3 (Γ) and 6 (Ϛ) can be confused, a suggestion made already in the early church; (2) John counts from midnight, the Roman legal day; (3) both are rough, since people reckoned time by the sun's position, and the third and sixth hours each covered a span; (4) Mark's or John's times are theological, Mark's marking the watches of prayer and John's the hour the Passover lambs were killed. Only Mark has this verse; Matthew and Luke leave it out.

a: "The King of the Jews."
p: The charge, written up for all to see, is the title Pilate used. Mark's readers read it as true.
b: Romans sometimes made a condemned man carry a placard, or hung it on the cross, naming the crime. Mark gives the shortest wording; Matthew, Luke and John expand it, and John says it was written in Hebrew, Latin and Greek. The title closes the chain that began in 15:2: Pilate asked, the soldiers saluted, and now the cross itself proclaims it. Mark's readers knew the king they served had been enthroned this way.

a: one on his right and one on his left
t: On his right and on his left
p: James and John had asked to sit at Jesus' right and left in his glory (10:37). These are the places they asked for.
b: In 10:37 James and John asked, "in your glory, let one of us sit on your right and one on your left." Jesus answered that those places were for those for whom they had been prepared (10:40). Mark uses almost the same words here. Jesus' "glory" in Mark is the cross, and the men at his right and left are two bandits. The later addition of 15:28 (see the variant) links the scene with Isaiah 53:12, "counted with the rebels."

a: They shook their heads
p: The mockers act out Psalm 22:7: "they sneer with their lips and shake their heads."
b: Psalm 22:7 says, "All who see me make fun of me; they sneer with their lips and shake their heads." Lamentations 2:15 uses the gesture for passers-by mocking ruined Jerusalem. "Ha!" (οὐά) is a cry of mock admiration. The charge that Jesus would tear down the sanctuary, called false at the trial (14:58), returns here as a taunt, and within hours the sanctuary curtain will be torn (15:38).

a: Others he saved. Himself he cannot save.
p: The priests mean it as scorn. Mark's readers hear the gospel: he does not save himself so that he can save others.
b: "Save" in Mark covers healing and rescue (5:23, 28, 34; 6:56; 10:52) as well as final salvation (8:35; 13:13). The priests admit that Jesus saved others, and they are right that he will not save himself. Jesus had taught that whoever wants to save his life will lose it (8:35) and that the Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom (10:45). The taunts in 15:29–32 repeat the testing in the wilderness, "come down and prove it," which Mark's short testing scene (1:12–13) did not describe.

a: so that we can see and believe
p: Jesus refused to give the Pharisees a sign (8:11–12). Here they demand one again, and he gives none.
b: "The Messiah, the King of Israel" is the Jewish form of the title Pilate put as "King of the Jews." The leaders' demand, "come down so that we can see and believe," echoes the Pharisees' demand for a sign from heaven, which Jesus refused (8:11–12). In Mark, faith never rests on spectacle. The first person to confess Jesus as God's Son will do it not because he came down, but because of how he died (15:39).

a: darkness lay over the whole land
p: Amos warned of a day when God would make the sun go down at noon. Exodus tells of a darkness before the death of the firstborn.
b: Amos 8:9–10 announces a day when God will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in daylight, a day of mourning like mourning for an only son. In Exodus 10:22 a thick darkness covered Egypt for three days before the Passover. A solar eclipse is impossible at Passover, which falls at full moon. Readers have taken the darkness as a miracle, as a dust storm or heavy cloud, or as a theological sign of judgment and mourning; "the whole land" may mean Judea or the whole earth. See the views at Matthew 27:45.

a: "Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?"
t: Jesus' only word from the cross in Mark
p: Mark gives the cry in Aramaic: Psalm 22:1. It is the only thing Jesus says from the cross in Mark.
b: Mark keeps the Aramaic form Eloi; Matthew 27:46 has Eli, closer to the Hebrew of the psalm. Both translate it as Psalm 22:1: "My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?" It is the only time in Mark that Jesus addresses God as "God" rather than "Father." Readers differ on its meaning: a real cry of abandonment as he bears sin or judgment; a prayer of a righteous sufferer that, as Jews knew, goes on to praise God's rescue (Psalm 22:22–31); or both. Mark does not soften it. See also the views at Matthew 27:46, and the variant here, where Codex Bezae and some Old Latin copies read "why have you insulted me?"
orig: Ἐλωῒ ἐλωῒ λεμὰ σαβαχθάνι (Elōi elōi lema sabachthani); Aramaic

a: he's calling for Elijah
p: Bystanders hear "Eloi" as "Elijah," whom popular Jewish belief saw as a helper of the righteous in trouble.
b: "Eloi" and "Eli" sound like Elijah's name (Eliyahu). Popular Jewish stories, later collected in the Talmud, told of Elijah coming to rescue the pious in distress, and Malachi 4:5 promised his return before the day of the LORD. Mark's readers know what the bystanders do not: Elijah has already come, in John the Baptist, and was killed (9:11–13; 6:14–29). No Elijah will come to take Jesus down.

a: sour wine
p: Cheap sour wine was the soldiers' drink. Psalm 69:21 says, "they made me drink vinegar."
b: Sour wine (ὄξος) was the cheap vinegar-wine of soldiers and laborers. Psalm 69:21 laments, "when I was thirsty they made me drink vinegar." In Mark the offer comes with a taunt, "Let's see if Elijah is coming," so it may be cruel, or a way to keep him alive longer for the joke. In John 19:28–30 Jesus says "I am thirsty" and receives it. See Matthew 27:48.

a: gave a loud cry
t: A loud cry at the end
p: Crucified men usually died slowly and weakly. Jesus dies after a loud cry, and quickly enough to surprise Pilate (15:44).
b: Crucifixion killed by exhaustion, shock and suffocation, often over a day or more. A loud cry at the end was unusual, and it is part of what the centurion notices (15:39). Mark's verb ἐξέπνευσεν, "breathed out," is a plain word for dying, but some readers hear a play on πνεῦμα, "spirit, breath": the Spirit that came down on Jesus at his baptism (1:10) and the breath he now gives up. Matthew 27:50 says that he "let his spirit go."

a: the sanctuary curtain was torn in two
t: Torn: the heavens and the curtain
p: Mark uses the Greek verb σχίζω ("tear") only twice: the heavens torn at Jesus' baptism (1:10) and the curtain torn at his death.
b: At the start of Mark the heavens are "torn open," the Spirit comes down, and a voice says "You are my Son" (1:10–11). At the end the sanctuary curtain is torn, and a centurion says "God's Son" (15:39). Josephus says the great outer curtain of the sanctuary was embroidered with a picture of the heavens, which makes the link closer still (David Ulansey). Readers take the tearing as God's judgment on the Temple (13:2; 14:58), as an opened way to God's presence (Hebrews 10:19–20), as God leaving the sanctuary, or as revelation, God's hidden face shown in the crucified one. These meanings can stand together. Matthew 27:51 has the same verb, and its Plain says "split"; the Plain of Mark keeps "torn" here to show the link with 1:10, and gives other Greek verbs other English ("tear down" for καταλύω in 14:58 and 15:29; "ripped" for the high priest's clothes in 14:63).

a: This man really was God's Son!
p: The Greek has no "the." A Roman might mean "a son of a god." For Mark it is the climax of the whole Gospel.
b: The words υἱὸς θεοῦ have no article. In grammar, a noun before the verb without an article can still be definite (the point of E. C. Colwell's rule), so "the Son of God" is possible; "a son of God" is also possible, and a Roman soldier might have meant that Jesus was a divine man or hero. The emperor himself was called "son of a god" (divi filius). Some read the words as sarcasm. Most interpreters take them as Mark's climax: the Gospel opened with "the Son of God" (1:1), God called Jesus his Son at the baptism and transfiguration (1:11; 9:7), demons knew it (3:11; 5:7), but no human being said it until a Gentile soldier saw Jesus die. Matthew 27:54 has the same words; Luke 23:47 has "righteous."

a: Mary the mother of the younger James and of Joses
p: In 6:3 Jesus' brothers are named James and Joses. Is this Mary his mother? Mark does not say so.
b: Mark names the brothers of Jesus as "James, Joses, Judas and Simon" (6:3). Here a Mary is mother of "James the younger" (literally "the small") and Joses. A few modern readers think she is Jesus' mother, described by her other sons; most think the gap is too odd for that and that she is another Mary, perhaps the "Mary of Clopas" of John 19:25, as Jerome held (Against Helvidius), and that these are common names. On the question of Jesus' brothers, see the traditions card at Matthew 13 and the note at Matthew 27:56.

a: Salome
p: Only Mark names Salome at the cross and the tomb. Later Christian writings made her a prominent disciple.
b: Salome appears in the New Testament only here and at 16:1. Matthew 27:56 has "the mother of Zebedee's sons" in the same list, and many have identified her with Salome, though the Gospels do not say so. In the second century, Salome becomes a figure in other writings: a disciple who questions Jesus in the Gospel of Thomas and in the lost Gospel of the Egyptians quoted by Clement of Alexandria (a Greek work, not the Coptic book of the same name found at Nag Hammadi), and a midwife in the Protevangelium of James. These later works are not in any church's Bible and are not sources for Mark's Salome.

a: These women had followed him and served him
p: "Followed" and "served" are the words of discipleship in Mark. The men ran; the women stayed.
b: "Follow" (ἀκολουθέω) is Mark's word for discipleship (1:18; 2:14; 8:34; 10:52), and "serve" (διακονέω) is the word Jesus used of himself: the Son of Man came to serve, not to be served (10:45). Mark uses both of these women, and only now tells the reader that they had been there from Galilee. They watch his death (15:40), his burial (15:47) and come to his tomb (16:1). In a world where women's testimony was little valued, the Gospels make them the witnesses to the central events. See Matthew 27:55.

a: the Day of Preparation, which is the day before the Sabbath
p: "Preparation" was the Jewish name for Friday. Mark explains it for readers who did not know.
b: Παρασκευή, "Preparation," was the day to get ready for the Sabbath, and it is still the word for Friday in modern Greek. Mark explains it with another word, προσάββατον, "pre-Sabbath," for Gentile readers. Deuteronomy 21:23 says a hanged body "must not stay on the tree overnight," and on a Sabbath eve the burial was urgent. Romans often left crucified bodies to rot as a warning, but Josephus says that Jews took down and buried even the crucified before sunset, and in Judea the authorities seem to have allowed it.

a: a council member of high standing
p: A member of the council that condemned Jesus asks for his body. Was he a secret disciple, or a pious Jew doing his duty?
b: Mark said that "all" the council condemned Jesus (14:64), yet here is a council member. Luke 23:51 adds that he had not agreed with their decision; Matthew 27:57 and John 19:38 call him a disciple, John a secret one. Mark says only that he was "looking for the kingdom of God," like devout Jews such as Simeon and Anna (Luke 2:25, 38). Raymond Brown argued that in Mark Joseph acts as a pious Jew who obeys the Law's command to bury the dead before night, not yet as a follower. "Boldly": asking for the body of a man executed for treason was dangerous.

a: Pilate wondered whether he could be dead already
p: Pilate checks with the centurion. Mark leaves no doubt that Jesus was dead.
b: Crucified men often lived for a day or more, so a death after about six hours surprised Pilate. Mark alone tells how he called the centurion to confirm it. The scene answers in advance the later "swoon" theory, that Jesus only fainted on the cross and revived in the tomb, which medical writers on crucifixion also reject. Some manuscripts read "whether he was already dead" instead of "whether he had died long ago"; the sense is the same.

a: the corpse
p: Joseph asked for Jesus' "body"; Pilate hands over a "corpse." Mark uses the blunt word on purpose.
b: In 15:43 Joseph asks for τὸ σῶμα, "the body." Mark then calls it τὸ πτῶμα, "the corpse," the word used for John the Baptist's remains (6:29) and for fallen carcasses. Later copyists (followed by the KJV) changed it back to "body." Mark's word underlines that Jesus was truly dead. Pilate "gave" it as a favor (δωρέομαι), with no fee.

a: a tomb carved out of the rock
p: Wealthy Jerusalem families buried their dead in tombs cut in the rock, closed with a stone across the door.
b: Many such tombs from the first century survive around Jerusalem: a small doorway cut into the rock, a chamber with niches or benches for bodies, and later a gathering of bones into ossuaries. Most were closed with a square block; round rolling stones were rarer and belonged to richer tombs (Amos Kloner). Mark's "rolled a stone up against" fits either. The Church of the Holy Sepulchre stands over a rock-cut tomb area that was outside the city wall in Jesus' day. See Matthew 27:60.

a: watched to see where he had been put
p: The same women see Jesus die, see where he is laid, and find the tomb empty. They did not go to the wrong tomb.
b: Mark names the women at the cross (15:40), at the burial (15:47) and at the tomb (16:1). The chain of witnesses answers the suggestion, made by some skeptics, that the women went to the wrong grave. Paul's early list of resurrection witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:3–8) names no women, perhaps because their testimony carried little weight in law, which makes it more striking that all four Gospels put women first at the tomb.

a: bought fragrant spices
p: The women come to finish what the hurried burial left undone. John says the body had already been spiced.
b: Jewish custom washed and anointed the dead before burial; the Mishnah even allows it on the Sabbath (Mishnah Shabbat 23:5). Mark mentions no anointing at the burial (15:46), so the women bought spices when the shops opened after the Sabbath ended at sunset on Saturday, and came at dawn. John 19:39–40 says Nicodemus brought a large amount of myrrh and aloes for the burial, which Mark does not mention. Anointing a body after a day and a half in a warm climate shows love more than practical sense. In Mark, Jesus' body has already been anointed in advance (14:8).

a: Very early on the first day of the week
p: "Very early" and "with the sun now up" pull against each other. Mark likes double time phrases.
b: "Very early" (λίαν πρωΐ) suggests before dawn, while "the sun having risen" suggests just after. Mark often gives a time twice, the second narrowing the first (1:32, 35; 14:12; 15:42), so he probably means "at first light, as the sun was coming up." John 20:1 says it was still dark. "The first day of the week" is Sunday; early Christians called it "the Lord's day" (Revelation 1:10) and met on it (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2).

a: a young man sitting on the right
p: Mark says a "young man" in white. Matthew calls him an angel; Luke has two men, John two angels.
b: White clothing marks heavenly beings (Daniel 7:9; 9:3), and angels can appear as young men: in 2 Maccabees 3:26, 33 two splendidly dressed young men are sent by God. Matthew 28:2–5 makes it "an angel of the Lord." Mark's choice of νεανίσκος, the same word as the young man who fled naked in 14:51–52, has led many to see a deliberate pair: one who flees, stripped, and one who sits clothed in white, perhaps a picture of the believer's death and new life in baptism. He sits "on the right," the side of honor and favor.

a: the one who was crucified
p: The Greek is a perfect participle: "the one who has been crucified." The risen Jesus is still the crucified one.
b: Mark writes τὸν ἐσταυρωμένον, a perfect passive participle, which describes a past act with a lasting result. Paul uses the same form: "Jesus Christ, and him crucified" (1 Corinthians 2:2; Galatians 3:1). The young man does not say "the one who was dead" but names him by the cross, then announces, "He has been raised," a passive that points to God as the one who raised him. In Mark the risen Lord never stops being the one who was crucified.

a: and Peter
p: Only Mark names Peter here. The man who denied Jesus three times is singled out for the message.
b: Matthew 28:7 says only "his disciples." Mark adds "and Peter," whose last scene was his tears after the denial (14:72). The early creed Paul quotes says the risen Jesus "appeared to Cephas," Peter's Aramaic name, "then to the Twelve" (1 Corinthians 15:5), and Luke 24:34 also says he appeared to Simon. Papias, about AD 120, said Mark wrote down what Peter taught; if so, the words "and Peter" are a quiet mark of forgiveness in the Gospel built on his memories.

a: shaking and shock
p: The second word is ekstasis, being beside oneself. It is the awe of people who have met God's power.
b: "Shaking and shock" renders τρόμος καὶ ἔκστασις. Ekstasis is literally "standing outside oneself": overwhelming amazement. Mark used it when Jairus's daughter rose (5:42). Fear and amazement are the usual response to God's acts in Mark: the disciples after the storm (4:41), the townspeople after the healing of the man from the tombs (5:15), the three at the transfiguration (9:6). Matthew 28:8 has the women run "frightened and full of joy at once."

a: they told no one anything
p: All through Mark, people told to be silent could not stop talking (1:44–45; 7:36). Now, told to speak, the women say nothing.
b: The double negative (οὐδενὶ οὐδέν, "to no one nothing") is emphatic. Mark's story has been full of people ordered to keep quiet who spread the news anyway (1:44–45; 7:36). Now that the time for silence is over (9:9), the messengers are silent.
