Some readers think Mark means only that they said nothing to anyone on the way, before reaching the disciples, as Matthew 28:8 and Luke 24:9 report; others take it as Mark's last, deliberate irony, which the reader is meant to overcome by speaking.

a: afraid
p: The oldest manuscripts end Mark here, with the Greek word gar, "for." Did Mark mean to stop?
b: The last words are ἐφοβοῦντο γάρ, "they were afraid, for." Ending a sentence with γάρ is rare but possible in Greek, and Pieter van der Horst showed in 1972 that whole works could end so. Three main views: (1) Mark meant to end here, leaving readers to answer the promise of 16:7 themselves (R. H. Lightfoot, Frank Kermode, J. Lee Magness, many recent scholars). (2) The ending was lost, perhaps from a damaged last page (N. Clayton Croy; R. T. France thought this likely). (3) Mark never finished. The longer endings were written later because many readers felt the story could not end this way. See the deep dives on this chapter page.

a: Having risen early on the first day of the week
t: A new beginning, in a different style
p: These verses start over: Mary Magdalene is introduced again, and the words and style differ from Mark's.
b: Mark 16:1 already named Mary Magdalene, yet 16:9 introduces her as if for the first time, adds that seven demons had been driven out of her (from Luke 8:2), and drops the other women. The phrase for "first day of the week" differs from 16:2. Many words in 16:9–20 occur nowhere else in Mark, and Mark's favorite words ("immediately," "again") are missing. The story summarizes appearances told in Luke, John and Acts. Most scholars conclude that a later writer composed these verses, probably in the early second century. See the variant, and the deep dive on this chapter page.

a: who were grieving and weeping
p: The scene matches John 20:18, where Mary Magdalene tells the disciples, "I have seen the Lord."
b: John 20:11–18 tells how the risen Jesus met Mary Magdalene alone at the tomb and sent her to the disciples. The longer ending gives a short form of the same story. "Grieving and weeping" fits the disciples' state in Luke 24:17 and John 16:20, where Jesus had foretold that they would weep and mourn and their grief would turn to joy.

a: two of them were walking out into the countryside
p: This is a summary of Luke 24:13–35, where two disciples walking to Emmaus meet Jesus and do not recognize him.
b: Luke tells at length how two disciples, one named Cleopas, walked to the village of Emmaus, talked with a stranger who explained the Scriptures, and recognized Jesus when he broke bread. "In a different form" explains why they did not recognize him (Luke 24:16 says their eyes were kept from recognizing him). The longer ending's writer seems to know Luke's story and to compress it into one sentence.

a: The rest did not believe them either.
p: In Luke the eleven are already saying "The Lord has risen" when the two return. Here no one believes them.
b: Luke 24:33–35 says that when the two came back from Emmaus, the eleven greeted them with the news that the Lord had appeared to Simon. The longer ending says the rest did not believe them. Writers since Augustine have tried to harmonize the accounts (some believed, some did not). The longer ending's repeated stress on unbelief (16:11, 13, 14) prepares for the rebuke in 16:14 and the call to believe in 16:16.

a: hard-heartedness
p: The word is sklērokardia, "hardness of heart." In Mark the disciples' hearts were hard before (6:52; 8:17).
b: Jesus used σκληροκαρδία, "hard-heartedness," of the attitude behind the divorce law (10:5), and Mark described the disciples' hearts as hardened when they failed to understand the loaves (6:52; 8:17). The longer ending applies it to the eleven's refusal to believe the witnesses. It matches Luke 24:25, where Jesus calls two disciples slow of heart to believe, and John 20:24–29 (Thomas). In one ancient manuscript the disciples answer the rebuke at length; see the variant on this verse, the "Freer Logion."

a: proclaim the good news to every creature
p: The longer ending's commission is close to Matthew 28:19, Luke 24:47 and Acts 1:8, in its own words.
b: "Every creature" is literally "all the creation" (πάσῃ τῇ κτίσει), meaning every human being, though some have read it more widely (Romans 8:19–22). Colossians 1:23 uses the same Greek phrase: the good news proclaimed "in all creation under heaven." The command picks up Mark 13:10 and 14:9, where the good news is to be proclaimed to all nations and in the whole world. Compare Matthew 28:19 ("make all the nations into disciples") and Luke 24:47.

a: The one who has believed and been baptized will be saved.
p: Baptism is joined to faith here, but the second half condemns unbelief, not lack of baptism. Churches read it differently.
b: The pairing of faith and baptism echoes Acts 2:38, 8:12 and 1 Peter 3:21, and churches that teach baptism is necessary for salvation (Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Churches of Christ) cite this verse. Others note the change in the second half: the one who "has refused to believe" is condemned, with no mention of baptism, so faith is what saves and baptism follows it. Both sides also weigh the verse's place in a later ending (see the variant at 16:9). See the Where Christians differ card on this chapter page.
r: Acts 2:38; Acts 8:12; Acts 16:31–33; 1 Peter 3:21; John 3:5; John 3:18; Titus 3:5

a: They will speak in new tongues
p: Every sign in 16:17–18 has a match in Acts or Luke: demons driven out, tongues, snakes, healing.
b: Driving out demons in Jesus' name (Acts 16:18; Luke 10:17), speaking in tongues (Acts 2:4; 10:46; 19:6; 1 Corinthians 12–14), a snake's bite that does no harm (Acts 28:3–6; Luke 10:19), and laying hands on the sick (Acts 28:8; James 5:14) all appear in the earliest church. Only the deadly drink has no New Testament story; Papias, as quoted by Eusebius, told of Justus Barsabbas drinking poison and coming to no harm. "New tongues" is found only here. James Kelhoffer argues that the writer drew on Acts and other early traditions to assure readers that God confirmed the message with signs.
r: Acts 2:4; Acts 10:46; Acts 16:18; Acts 19:6; Acts 28:3–6; Acts 28:8; Luke 10:17–19; 1 Corinthians 12:10; James 5:14

a: They will take up snakes
p: A few Appalachian churches handle snakes in worship. Most churches read the verse as a promise, not a command.
b: In the early 1900s George Went Hensley, a preacher in Tennessee, began handling rattlesnakes in worship as a sign of faith, and a small movement of independent Holiness churches in Appalachia has continued the practice; several states have outlawed it, and dozens of handlers have died from bites. Ralph Hood and Paul Williamson have studied these churches closely. Nearly all churches, including the large Pentecostal bodies, read the verse as a promise of God's protection when danger comes unsought, as with Paul's viper on Malta (Acts 28:3–6), not a command to test God (Matthew 4:7). The verse's place in a later ending (see the variant at 16:9) also affects how much weight it is given.

a: he was taken up into heaven, and he sat down at God's right hand
t: Taken up like Elijah, seated as in Psalm 110
p: "Taken up" is the Greek Bible's word for Elijah's going to heaven. "At God's right hand" fulfills Psalm 110:1.
b: The verb ἀναλαμβάνω is used of Elijah in the Greek of 2 Kings 2:11 and of Jesus in Acts 1:2, 11, 22. Sitting at God's right hand fulfills Psalm 110:1, "Sit at my right hand," which Jesus quoted (12:36) and claimed before the high priest (14:62). Irenaeus, writing about AD 180, quoted this verse as from "the end of Mark's Gospel," the earliest clear witness that the longer ending was being read as part of Mark.

a: he backed up the word through the signs that followed
p: The ending closes with the Lord at work through the messengers, as in Acts 14:3 and Hebrews 2:3–4.
b: Acts 14:3 says the Lord bore witness to the message of his grace by signs and wonders done by Paul and Barnabas, and Hebrews 2:3–4 says God confirmed the message with signs, wonders and miracles. The longer ending ends with the same picture: the ascended Lord is not absent but working with his messengers. Some scholars hear an echo of this verse in Justin Martyr's First Apology 45 (about AD 155), which speaks of the apostles going out and preaching everywhere; whether Justin knew the longer ending is debated.
